questions.q: Identify the tag, element, and attribute in this snippet: ``
questions.a: Tag: `` (self-closing tag). Element: the entire `` (since void elements have no closing tag, the element is just the tag with its attributes). Attributes: `src="photo.jpg"` and `alt="My photo"`. A wrong answer like calling `src` a "tag" or saying the element is just `photo.jpg` reveals confusion between the three vocabulary terms — students often conflate the attribute name with the tag name, or think the attribute value is the element content.

The tags are improperly nested — `` opens inside `

`. A student who says "it works in browser anyway" misunderstands that browsers perform error correction but the DOM tree becomes unpredictable; this exact error appears in CBSE board questions asking to "identify the error in the following code."

questions.q:
Compare these two snippets. Which produces semantically correct structure for a navigation menu and why? A) `
Home | About
` B) `
Home | About
`
questions.a: Snippet B is correct. `<nav>` is a semantic element that tells browsers, screen readers, and search engines "this is a navigation section." `<div>` is generic and carries no meaning. Students who pick A often think "both look the same" — missing that semantic HTML affects SEO, accessibility, and maintainability, which CBSE competency questions explicitly test.

questions.q: A student writes `<input required="false">` to make a field optional. Evaluate this approach and state the correct way to make an input optional.
questions.a: The approach is wrong. `required` is a **boolean attribute** — its presence alone means `true`; writing `required="false"` still makes it required because the attribute exists. To make it optional, simply omit the attribute: `<input>`. This is a classic JEE/NEET-style trap: boolean attributes in HTML5 follow "presence = true, absence = false" — no value needed. Students used to `checked="checked"` (XHTML style) often carry that habit incorrectly.
